passage: In the village near Tumkur, Amma cut the ripe mango into pieces on a steel plate. Shankar, eleven, leaned close. "Lokesh got the big piece with the seed!" Lokesh, nine, grabbed it. "You got two pieces yesterday!" "And you slept later on Sunday!" "You got new chappals first!" Amma put down the knife. The boys were not looking at the mango anymore; they were looking at her, waiting to see whose side she would take. Shankar's voice cracked a little. "You always give him more." Amma looked at the two of them, their faces fierce, and understood it wasn't really about mango at all.

qa.q: What was Amma cutting on the steel plate?
qa.a: She was cutting the ripe mango into pieces.

qa.q: What does Shankar's cracked voice suggest he really wants?
qa.a: It suggests he feels hurt and less loved, and wants to know he matters to Amma as much as Lokesh does, not just a bigger piece of mango.

qa.q: What could Amma do at this turning point?
qa.a: Instead of weighing pieces, she could reassure each boy of her love and give each some time alone with her, which answers the real need.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see the mango fight?
qa.a: Lokesh probably feels he is the one treated unfairly, remembering Shankar's two pieces yesterday.

grounding: It shows two children keeping count of shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact equality, when underneath they need to know they matter equally.

passage: In their Melbourne flat, Valentina, eleven, stood at the fridge with a notebook. "Mei got a new phone case and I didn't. That's three things this month." Mei, nine, ran in. "You stayed up till nine-thirty on Friday! I had to sleep at nine!" "Because I'm older!" "You got the bigger slice of pizza!" Their father looked up from the stove. "Are you two keeping score?" Valentina held up her notebook proudly. It had columns: Mei, Me. He sat down at the table. "What would it mean if Mei got more?" Valentina's face changed. She said quietly, "That you like her more." Mei looked at her sister, surprised. "I thought you thought that about me."

qa.q: What columns did Valentina's notebook have?
qa.a: It had two columns: Mei and Me.

qa.q: What does Valentina's quiet answer reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: It reveals she is worried her father likes Mei more, so keeping score is really about feeling she matters.

qa.q: Why was the father's question a good turning point?
qa.a: Asking what it would mean if Mei got more helped Valentina say the real worry, so he can reassure both girls rather than count things.

qa.q: What does Mei's reply show about how she sees things?
qa.a: It shows Mei had the same fear, thinking she was the one who mattered less.

grounding: It illustrates siblings counting shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact fairness, when underneath each needs to know they matter as much.
